title: inherit-brain on HERB, held-out run
outcome_sentence: On Salesforce's HERB questions, 40.8 points above an agent using the same model, no worse than 3 points below reading the whole product, with 8.0% of its tokens, and a path behind every answer.

A5.description: The company brain: nine read-only tools on the FalkorDB graph (multi-hop queries, aggregation across cards, algorithms), driven by the shared agent loop. The 'if this person leaves' counterfactual is a separate feature and was not part of the scored run.

A0.description: The HERB paper's retrieval agent over the raw records, run in the shared loop with the same limits (12 tool calls, 60,000 input tokens). The comparator of H1: same model, no graph.

A1f.description: Reading the whole product: one model call whose context holds all of the product's records (about 110,000 to 140,000 tokens). The comparator of H2.

A0v.description: The HERB paper's hybrid RAG with a single retrieval (BM25 top 20, then vector top 20) and one model call over those chunks, no tools, no loop.

A4.description: Typed depth-1 access to the entity cards (resolve, get_card, neighbors), with exact aggregation; the restricted card view. Five products plus the multi-hop questions.

A4c.description: The same cards and depth-1 tools, with the model assembling multi-hop answers step by step. Five products.

A0f.description: Retrieval over the pre-extracted entity cards with the shared loop: the A0 agent on the card representation. Five products.

A2.description: GraphRAG-SDK 1.4.0 with its automatic ontology, one model call over its retrieved context. Six sampled products.

arm_note: A4, A4c and A0f ran on five seeded held-out products (A4 also on the 7 multi-hop questions); A2 on six sampled products. Their columns are not comparable to the full arms; the contrasts pair them with A5 or A0 on the same questions.

hypotheses.comparison: A5 minus A4 on every question A4 answered

how_differences_are_read: A0f minus A0: the effect of the pre-extracted representation on a retrieval agent (representation and retrieved content change together).
A4 minus A0f: the same cards, typed access and exact aggregation against retrieval.
A5 minus A4: the full multi-hop toolkit (multi-hop queries, aggregation across cards, algorithms) against the restricted card view; not attributed to multi-hop alone.
A5 against A4c: multi-hop inside fixed tools against the model assembling it step by step (accuracy, calls, tokens, latency).
Every difference is measured under the registered resource limits. An arm that stops on its budget more often is not given more; budget-stop rates are reported per arm.
None of these differences shows that another database could not do the same.

post_hoc.title: Provider network errors
post_hoc.text: 44 of A0's and 6 of A1f's failures were the proxy's 502 upstream unreachable errors from the model provider, not the arms' own failures. They stay zero-scored in the main table, as registered. Dropping those slots from both arms of the pair:

post_hoc.title: Company answers given as customer ids
post_hoc.text: All arms were told to answer a company by its name, never its CUST- id; A1f gave CUST- ids in 49 of its 104 company answers (A0 in 3, A5 in none), which score 0 under the registered id matching. Mapping CUST- ids to company names through the customer directory, the same way for every arm, and rescoring with the same F1:

caveats: The judge is model M, so content and unanswerable scores are not comparable with the HERB paper's GPT-4o-judged numbers.
H3 rests on one multi-hop family with 7 held-out questions.
The loop arms share a 60,000-token input budget; an arm that runs out of budget is not given more.
Scores are F1 x 100 (ids) or the HERB judge on model M (content, unanswerable). Failed slots are scored 0 and kept in the denominator.
